sets.title: A revised deadline
sets.directions: Listen to the message and choose the correct answer.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.voiceCue: Neutral British woman; clear exam pace
segments.text: You hear a project manager leaving a message for a colleague.

segments.speaker: Manager
segments.text: Hi, Elena. The client no longer needs the draft on Thursday, which gives us a little breathing room. They would still like the figures by Friday morning, though, so please send your spreadsheet before you leave on Thursday. I can then add the commentary and submit the complete report on Monday.

items.question: What does the manager ask Elena to do?

options.text: Send the complete report on Thursday
Provide the figures by Thursday evening
Write the report commentary on Friday

items.explanationZh: 經理要 Elena 在星期四下班前寄出試算表中的數字；完整報告則由經理加上評論後於星期一提交。

distractorRationales.A: 星期四只交數字，不是完整報告。
distractorRationales.C: 評論由經理撰寫，不是 Elena。

items.evidence: send your spreadsheet before you leave on Thursday

sets.title: Meeting-room problem
sets.directions: Listen to the conversation and choose the correct answer.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: You hear two colleagues discussing a meeting room.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: The projector in Room Four is working again, but the air conditioning is still being repaired.

segments.speaker: Woman
segments.text: Then let's move the supplier presentation to Room Seven. It's smaller, but the video screen is large enough, and I can bring in two extra chairs.

items.question: Why do the colleagues decide to use Room Seven?

options.text: Room Four will be uncomfortable.
Room Four has no presentation equipment.
Room Seven provides more seating.

items.explanationZh: Room Four 的投影機已修好，但空調仍在維修，因此可能不舒適。Room Seven 其實較小，還需要加椅子。

distractorRationales.B: 投影機已恢復運作。
distractorRationales.C: Room Seven 較小，座位不是優勢。

items.evidence: the air conditioning is still being repaired

sets.title: A delayed delivery
sets.directions: Listen to the call and choose the correct answer.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: You hear a customer speaking to an account manager.

segments.speaker: Customer
segments.text: I understand the storm delayed the shipment, and fortunately we still have enough stock for this week. What worries me is that nobody contacted us until I called this morning. A brief update yesterday would have allowed us to warn our own customers.

items.question: What is the customer's main complaint?

options.text: The reason given for the delay is unacceptable.
The company failed to communicate promptly.
The delay has left her company without stock.

items.explanationZh: 客戶接受暴風雨造成延誤，也說本週庫存足夠；真正不滿的是供應商沒有主動及時通知。

distractorRationales.A: 她表示理解暴風雨造成的延誤。
distractorRationales.C: 她明確說本週庫存仍足夠。

items.evidence: nobody contacted us until I called this morning

sets.title: Workshop preparation
sets.directions: Listen to the announcement and choose the correct answer.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: You hear part of an internal announcement.

segments.speaker: Trainer

options.text: A completed exercise
A printed case study
The original invitation email

distractorRationales.B: 現場會提供影本。

sets.title: Reviewing an interview day
sets.directions: Listen to the conversation and answer both questions.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Two managers are reviewing a recruitment day.

segments.speaker: Lena
segments.text: The candidates' presentations were stronger than I expected. The problem was our schedule. Asking people to complete the written task immediately after lunch meant the final interviews started nearly forty minutes late.

segments.speaker: Marcus
segments.text: True. We could shorten the written task next time.

segments.speaker: Lena
segments.text: I'd rather keep it as it is. It showed us how clearly they could organise complex information. We should run it while each person is waiting for their first interview instead.

segments.speaker: Marcus
segments.text: Good point. What about the group exercise? It was useful, but six candidates made the discussion hard to follow.

segments.speaker: Lena
segments.text: Let's use groups of four. We'll need an extra assessor, but the evidence will be much better.

items.question: What caused the interviews to run late?

options.text: The presentations lasted longer than planned.
The written activity was scheduled poorly.
The lunch break began later than expected.

items.explanationZh: 問題不是作業本身太長，而是所有人都在午餐後做，導致最後面試延誤。

distractorRationales.A: 只說簡報品質比預期好，未說超時。
distractorRationales.C: 沒有提到午休延誤。

items.evidence: completing the written task immediately after lunch meant the final interviews started ... late

items.question: What change do the managers agree to make?

options.text: Reduce the length of the written task
Remove the group exercise
Use smaller discussion groups

items.explanationZh: 兩人同意把小組人數從六人減為四人；Lena 明確反對縮短書面作業，也沒有要取消團體活動。

distractorRationales.A: Marcus 提議，但 Lena 不同意。
distractorRationales.B: 他們認為團體活動有用，只調整人數。

items.evidence: Let's use groups of four.

sets.title: Changing the launch message
sets.directions: Listen to the conversation and answer both questions.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: A marketing director and a product designer are discussing a launch.

segments.speaker: Director
segments.text: The campaign makes the device look impressively advanced, but our customer interviews suggest people are less interested in the technology itself than in avoiding complicated setup.

segments.speaker: Designer
segments.text: So rather than listing every feature, we show someone using it successfully within minutes?

segments.speaker: Director
segments.text: Exactly. The engineering team may feel we're underplaying their work, but ease of use is the clearest commercial advantage. Also, I'd postpone the influencer event. The latest software is stable, yet the packaging samples still look temporary.

segments.speaker: Designer
segments.text: The event venue charges a cancellation fee.

segments.speaker: Director
segments.text: A modest one. An event that makes the product feel unfinished would cost us far more.

items.question: How should the campaign change?

options.text: Emphasise simple operation rather than technical detail
Explain how the engineering team developed the product
Compare the number of features with competing devices

items.explanationZh: 訪談顯示顧客在乎避免複雜設定，因此宣傳重點要從技術功能轉為快速、容易上手。

distractorRationales.B: 工程團隊可能希望技術被看見，但不是商業訊息重點。
distractorRationales.C: 對話沒有建議與競品比較功能數量。

items.evidence: ease of use is the clearest commercial advantage

items.question: Why does the director want to postpone the event?

options.text: The software still contains serious faults.
The presentation of the product is not ready.
The cancellation fee has become more affordable.

items.explanationZh: 軟體已穩定，但包裝樣品仍像臨時版本，可能讓產品看起來未完成，因此延期。

distractorRationales.A: 對話明說軟體已穩定。
distractorRationales.C: 費用只是可接受的代價，不是延期原因。

items.evidence: the packaging samples still look temporary

sets.title: A manager explains a pilot policy
sets.directions: Listen to the talk and answer the five questions in order.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: A department manager is explaining a new remote-work pilot.

segments.speaker: Manager
segments.text: Thanks for joining. From next month, our department will test a revised hybrid-working arrangement for twelve weeks. This isn't a response to poor productivity; output has remained high. The issue is that different teams currently choose office days independently, so people often travel in for meetings that still happen entirely online. Under the pilot, Tuesdays will be our shared office day. Teams may select one additional day if their work benefits from face-to-face contact, but nobody is expected to attend simply to answer emails at a different desk. We considered Thursday as the common day because the building is quieter then. However, customer-support data showed that Tuesday has the fewest urgent calls, making it easier for that team to participate. To judge the pilot, we will compare project turnaround times and ask staff about the quality of collaboration. We will not treat desk occupancy as a measure of success. Some colleagues have asked whether travel costs will be reimbursed. Our existing policy remains unchanged: normal commuting is not covered, but journeys to another branch for a scheduled meeting are. Finally, please record practical difficulties in the short weekly form. Don't wait until the final survey; small issues are easier to fix while the pilot is running.

items.question: Why is the pilot being introduced?

options.text: Staff productivity has fallen.
Office attendance is poorly coordinated.
Online meetings are being discontinued.

items.explanationZh: 目前各團隊自行決定到辦日，造成有人進辦公室卻仍全程線上開會；核心問題是協調不足。

distractorRationales.A: 經理明說產出仍高。
distractorRationales.C: 並非停止線上會議。

items.evidence: different teams currently choose office days independently

items.question: Why was Tuesday chosen as the shared office day?

options.text: More desks are available.
Most project meetings already occur then.
Customer-support demand is usually lower.

items.explanationZh: 星期二緊急客服來電最少，因此客服團隊較能參加共同到辦日。

distractorRationales.A: 較安靜、空間較多的是星期四的考量，但未被採用。
distractorRationales.B: 未提到既有專案會議時間。

items.evidence: Tuesday has the fewest urgent calls

items.question: What may teams do in addition to attending on Tuesday?

options.text: Choose another useful office day
Replace Tuesday with a different day
Work from another branch every week

items.explanationZh: 團隊若面對面工作有助益，可以再選一天；不能取代共同的星期二。

distractorRationales.B: Tuesday 是共同到辦日。
distractorRationales.C: 另一分公司只在差旅規定中出現。

items.evidence: select one additional day if their work benefits

items.question: Which measure will NOT be used to evaluate the pilot?

options.text: Project completion speed
Staff views on collaboration
The number of occupied desks

items.explanationZh: 經理明確說不會把座位使用率當成功指標。

distractorRationales.A: 會比較專案 turnaround times。
distractorRationales.B: 會詢問員工對合作品質的看法。

items.evidence: We will not treat desk occupancy as a measure of success.

items.question: What does the manager ask staff to do during the pilot?

options.text: Submit problems each week
Claim ordinary commuting expenses
Save all feedback for the final survey

items.explanationZh: 員工應每週用短表記錄實務問題，讓團隊能及早修正。

distractorRationales.B: 一般通勤不補助。
distractorRationales.C: 經理要求不要等到最後調查。

items.evidence: record practical difficulties in the short weekly form

sets.title: Five employees suggest improvements
sets.directions: Listen to five employees. Match each speaker with the main improvement they want.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: You will hear five employees discussing one improvement they would make at work.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: The online courses are useful, but people complete them alone and rarely discuss what they've learned. A monthly session where colleagues demonstrate one practical technique would turn that information into something we actually use.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Our desks and equipment are fine. What wastes time is discovering that two teams have arranged client calls in neighbouring rooms. A central booking calendar showing which rooms are suitable for quiet calls would solve most of it.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Managers often thank us at the end of a large project, which is appreciated. I'd rather hear brief comments while the work is still in progress, though. Then we could adjust before the final deadline instead of learning afterwards what should have changed.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4

segments.speaker: Speaker 5

sets.title: Three managers describe difficult decisions
sets.directions: Listen to three managers. For each speaker, identify the situation and the lesson learned.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Three managers describe a difficult decision.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: A major customer asked us to deliver three weeks early. I agreed before checking with production because I was afraid of appearing unhelpful. We met the date, but only by delaying two smaller orders. I learned that protecting one relationship at the expense of several others is not good customer service.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: When our analyst left unexpectedly, I divided her reports among the rest of the team. Everyone was already busy, but hiring a contractor seemed expensive. Two months later, overtime and errors had cost more than temporary help would have done. Short-term savings need to be compared with hidden operational costs.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: We had to choose between improving an existing service and launching a new one. I relied heavily on a survey whose respondents were mostly current customers, so naturally they favoured improvements. Later research showed a new market we had missed. Evidence is valuable only if you understand whose views are absent.

sharedOptions.text: Consider who is missing from the evidence
Avoid commitments before checking wider effects
Include indirect costs in financial decisions

sets.title: Why a process redesign succeeded
sets.directions: Read the article and answer the five questions.

stimulus.text:
When Northbridge Insurance redesigned its claims process, senior managers initially assumed that new software would deliver most of the improvement. A six-week observation study suggested otherwise. Claims handlers were spending almost a quarter of their time requesting information that customers believed they had already supplied. The problem was not missing technology but inconsistent wording: different teams used different names for the same documents.

Instead of purchasing the proposed system immediately, Northbridge created a cross-functional group of claims staff, customer-service advisers and legal specialists. The group produced a shared vocabulary and rewrote customer instructions. Managers expected resistance because standardisation can be interpreted as limiting professional judgement. Yet staff welcomed the change once they saw that the new wording removed repetitive enquiries without determining how complex cases should be assessed.

The company then ran a controlled trial in two branches. Processing time fell by 18 per cent, but the more revealing result was a reduction in cases returned to customers for additional information. This mattered because returned cases had been a major source of customer frustration, even when total processing time was reasonable.

Northbridge eventually introduced a smaller software upgrade to support the revised process. According to the operations director, technology was valuable because it reinforced decisions already tested by staff, not because it replaced the need to understand the work. She argues that organisations often reverse this order: they buy a system and only afterwards ask employees to reshape their work around it.

items.question: What did the observation study reveal?

options.text: Customers regularly refused to provide documents.
Terminology differences were creating repeated work.
Claims staff needed more legal training.

items.explanationZh: 不同團隊對同一文件使用不同名稱，造成客戶以為已提供、員工卻再次索取的重工。

distractorRationales.A: 問題是理解不一致，不是拒絕。
distractorRationales.C: 法律專家參與小組，但研究未說員工缺乏法律訓練。

items.evidence: different teams used different names for the same documents

items.question: Why did managers anticipate resistance?

options.text: Staff might see standardisation as restricting their expertise.
The proposed language was legally difficult to understand.
Employees had already chosen a different software system.

items.explanationZh: 管理者擔心標準化會被理解成限制專業判斷。

distractorRationales.B: 法務人員協助，但沒有說文字難懂。
distractorRationales.C: 員工未選擇另一系統。

items.evidence: interpreted as limiting professional judgement

stimulus.text:
A mentoring programme can connect less-experienced employees with colleagues who understand the organisation. {{1}} Without that clarity, meetings can become pleasant conversations that produce little change.

sets.title: A library's tool-lending project
sets.directions: Listen to the interview and answer the five questions in order.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: A radio presenter is interviewing a librarian about a new service.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: Maya, why has the library started lending tools?

segments.speaker: Maya
segments.text: Residents told us they wanted to repair household items but didn't own equipment they might use only once. Some could afford the tools, but considered the purchase wasteful; others had nowhere to store them. We first imagined a simple shelf of donated tools. Safety advice changed our thinking: every item needed inspection, clear instructions and a reliable record of previous use. Donated equipment sometimes arrived without guards, manuals or even a clear model number, so a volunteer could not responsibly approve it just because it appeared to work. We began with forty new or professionally checked items rather than accepting everything people offered. The most popular objects aren't the electric drills, as we predicted, but basic carpet cleaners and long ladders. Booking patterns show that these are often reserved for a specific weekend task and returned immediately afterwards. That tells us the service is helping with occasional practical jobs, not replacing equipment used by professionals. Anyone with a library card can borrow most tools after watching a ten-minute safety video. Cutting equipment requires an additional in-person demonstration. Items are normally lent for four days. We considered a deposit, but that could exclude people the project is intended to help, so late returns are handled by temporarily suspending further borrowing. Someone who contacts us before the deadline may receive an extension if nobody else has booked the item. Next spring we hope to run repair workshops. These won't be classes where an expert fixes things for you; participants will bring an object and learn alongside volunteers how to diagnose the problem. The aim is to make the reasoning visible, including the decision to stop when a repair requires professional knowledge. Our biggest challenge now is storage. Demand justifies expanding the collection, but there is little unused space in the present building.

sets.title: Five students describe a useful study change
sets.directions: Listen to five students. Match each speaker with the study change that helped them most.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Five students describe a change that improved their studying.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: I used to highlight almost every sentence, which made revision slow and confusing. The bright pages looked familiar, but I could not explain the ideas without seeing them. Now, after each section, I close the book and write three questions that the section should help me answer. I return to those questions the following day. Testing myself later shows immediately what I haven't understood and stops me mistaking recognition for real knowledge.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Long weekend sessions looked impressive on my calendar but rarely happened. If friends made plans or I felt tired, the entire week's study disappeared. Twenty-five minutes before breakfast is much easier to protect because nobody expects me to be available then. The amount is small, yet doing it every day has made a bigger difference, and missing one morning no longer feels like complete failure.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: I was reluctant to show anyone unfinished work because I thought comments would be useful only after I had made the writing presentable. Joining a group where we exchange rough drafts changed that. We respond to the central idea rather than correcting every sentence. Early comments can prevent hours spent developing the wrong argument, while I still make the final decisions about the wording.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: I kept revising topics I already enjoyed, so study felt productive even when I was avoiding the weakest areas. I now use my quiz results to choose the next subject, starting with the lowest score even when it isn't appealing. I set a small target before switching topics, which makes the difficult material manageable. My improvement has become much more balanced rather than depending on what I happen to like.

segments.speaker: Speaker 5
segments.text: Online lectures tempted me to answer messages at the same time, and keeping the slides open encouraged me to read ahead instead of following the explanation. Downloading the audio and walking in a quiet park means I actually listen. I pause only when an idea needs thought, then make brief voice notes afterwards rather than trying to type while moving. Back home, I check those notes against the slides.

Selecting topics according to test performance
Getting feedback before work is complete
Listening while away from digital distractions

sets.title: Three people reflect on volunteering
sets.directions: Listen to three people. For each speaker, identify the activity and the unexpected benefit.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.text: Three people discuss volunteering.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: I joined a team recording spoken versions of local news for people with limited sight. I expected the main challenge to be reading clearly and keeping a steady pace. In fact, we first have to decide which reports matter and shorten them without changing their meaning. Choosing what to include taught me to recognise biased language and separate fact from opinion much more carefully. I now notice when a headline presents an assumption as if it were evidence.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: I help maintain paths in a nature reserve, clearing drainage channels and replacing damaged signs. I signed up for outdoor exercise, not conversation, and assumed everyone would quietly concentrate on the physical work. Yet tasks are done in pairs that change each week. Working beside people of very different ages has made me much more comfortable speaking to strangers, which has even helped at university when I need to join an unfamiliar discussion group.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: At the community kitchen I organise donated ingredients before the cooks arrive. We check dates, group similar items and identify anything that must be used immediately. The quantities change every week, so fixed recipes rarely work and an ingredient promised in the morning may never arrive. Finding sensible substitutions has made me far more inventive with meals at home, where I now plan around what is already available and waste much less food.

More confidence communicating with unfamiliar people
More creative use of available resources

sets.title: Why ordinary observations matter
sets.directions: Choose the sentence that best fits each gap. There are extra sentences.

stimulus.text:
Citizen-science projects invite members of the public to collect or classify information for research. Their value is not simply that volunteers provide free labour. {{1}} A professional research team could never be present in all those places at once.

The most successful projects make the task specific. Asking people to report whether they enjoyed a walk may produce interesting comments, but the information is hard to compare. {{2}} Consistent observations can then be combined meaningfully.

Training is still essential, even when the task appears simple. Volunteers may interpret colours, quantities or animal behaviour differently. {{3}} Short practice examples with feedback often improve accuracy substantially.

Researchers also need to explain what happens to the data. People lose motivation if observations disappear into a database without any visible result. {{4}} Maps, regular updates and explanations of unexpected findings show that each contribution forms part of a larger investigation.

Finally, citizen science should not be presented as a replacement for professional expertise. {{5}} The partnership works best when public participation expands the reach of carefully designed research.

They can observe changes across huge areas and over long periods.

sets.title: Learning at a repair café
sets.directions: Listen to the extended recording and answer the five questions. The information follows the question order.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.voiceCue: Neutral British woman; clear exam pace
segments.text: You hear a radio presenter interviewing the coordinator of a repair café.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: Lena, what persuaded you to start a repair café in your neighbourhood?

segments.speaker: Lena
segments.text: The immediate trigger was a survey showing how many small electrical items residents threw away. Yet the survey also revealed that many people wanted to repair things but felt embarrassed by how little they knew. So our purpose was not simply to prevent waste. We wanted to create a place where asking a basic question felt normal rather than foolish.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: Did the first sessions work as you expected?

segments.speaker: Lena
segments.text: Not at all. We assumed skilled volunteers would fix objects while owners watched. The room quickly became a queue of silent customers, and the volunteers were exhausted. We changed the rule: the owner now stays at the table, describes the fault and performs any safe step they can manage. Repairs sometimes take longer, but people leave with knowledge they can use again.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: Why do visitors need to book when the service is free?

segments.speaker: Lena
segments.text: Booking is mainly about matching. A volunteer comfortable with sewing machines may know nothing about digital radios. The form asks what the object is and how it failed, so we can schedule the right expertise. We reserve two walk-in places because not everyone can plan ahead, but accepting unlimited arrivals would produce long waits and rushed safety checks.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: Has anything surprised you since making those changes?

segments.speaker: Lena
segments.text: Yes—the largest benefit may be social. Some retired volunteers originally joined to practise technical skills. They now say that explaining a repair to a nervous stranger gives them a stronger sense of usefulness. Visitors also exchange advice while waiting, so the café has connected people who had lived on the same street for years without speaking.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: And what would you like to improve next?

segments.speaker: Lena
segments.text: We need better evidence about what happens afterwards. Counting successful repairs tells us little about whether an item survives another month or whether its owner attempts a future repair. We are designing a brief follow-up message that asks both questions without making people complete a long survey. That should show whether we are building lasting confidence, not merely rescuing objects for a few weeks.

items.question: What broader need led Lena to establish the repair café?

options.text: Residents needed a cheaper place to buy appliances
People lacked confidence to learn practical repair skills
Retired technicians wanted formal teaching work
The council required households to reduce electrical use

items.explanationZh: 丟棄物品只是表面問題；更深層需求是居民想學修理，卻因缺乏知識而不好意思提問。

distractorRationales.A: 咖啡館不是販售家電。
distractorRationales.C: 退休志工的收穫是後來出現的結果，不是創辦原因。
distractorRationales.D: 主題是廢棄物，不是降低用電。

items.evidence: wanted to repair things but felt embarrassed by how little they knew

items.question: What did the organisers change after the first sessions?

options.text: They made owners participate in the repair process
They limited the service to easily repaired objects
They replaced volunteers who worked too slowly
They began charging customers who only watched

items.explanationZh: 原本是志工修、物主旁觀，後來改為物主必須共同說明與操作安全步驟，重點轉向學習。

distractorRationales.B: 沒有把服務限於簡單物品。
distractorRationales.C: 問題是運作模式，不是志工速度。

items.evidence: owner now stays at the table

items.question: What is the main purpose of the booking form?

options.text: To estimate the likely cost of replacement parts
To decide whether an object is worth repairing
To connect each problem with suitable knowledge
To give regular visitors priority over newcomers

items.explanationZh: 表單先取得物品及故障資訊，目的在安排具相符專長的志工。

distractorRationales.A: 沒有用表單估零件費。
distractorRationales.B: 不是先篩掉不值得修的物品。
distractorRationales.D: 仍保留 walk-in 名額，沒有常客優先。

items.evidence: schedule the right expertise

items.question: What unexpected outcome does Lena describe?

options.text: The café has strengthened relationships in the area
Visitors now repair most items without any help
Volunteers prefer social activities to technical work
People have started donating large amounts of equipment

items.explanationZh: 最意外的不是修理數量，而是志工與訪客建立用途感、鄰居彼此開始交流。

distractorRationales.B: 訪客仍在志工協助下修理。
distractorRationales.C: 志工仍使用技術，只是同時獲得社交價值。

items.evidence: connected people who had lived on the same street for years without speaking

items.question: What does Lena hope the follow-up message will reveal?

options.text: Whether visitors would pay for future sessions
Whether repairs and confidence continue beyond the visit
Which volunteers receive the highest customer ratings
Which types of object take the longest to fix

items.explanationZh: 她想追蹤物品是否持續可用，以及物主日後是否敢自己再修，評估長期效果。

distractorRationales.A: 服務付費不是追蹤重點。
distractorRationales.C: 不是志工排名。
distractorRationales.D: 現場修理時間不是她說缺少的證據。

items.evidence: whether an item survives another month or whether its owner attempts a future repair

sets.title: Rethinking light after dark
sets.directions: Listen to the extended recording and answer the five questions. The information follows the question order.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.voiceCue: Neutral British woman; clear exam pace
segments.text: You hear part of a podcast about a neighbourhood lighting project.

segments.speaker: Host
segments.text: When residents in the Brookfield district first asked for better lighting, the request sounded straightforward. Several routes between the station and nearby housing felt unsafe after dark, and the natural response was to install brighter lamps everywhere. Urban designer Marcus Lee explains why the council paused before doing that.

segments.speaker: Marcus
segments.text: We walked the area with residents rather than measuring brightness alone. People were not consistently afraid of darkness. They were uneasy where sudden contrasts prevented them from seeing who was ahead, or where overgrown plants created hiding places. In fact, one extremely bright car park made the adjoining footpath appear darker. That finding shifted the project from increasing light to improving visual continuity.

segments.speaker: Host
segments.text: The team then tested a temporary scheme on two streets.

segments.speaker: Marcus
segments.text: We lowered the strongest lamp, added several modest lights at eye level and cut back selected vegetation. The equipment was mounted temporarily so residents could comment before anything became permanent. We deliberately left a nearby street unchanged. Comparing the two routes helped us separate the effect of the design from seasonal changes, such as more commuters travelling after sunset.

segments.speaker: Host
segments.text: One response to the trial was not anticipated.

segments.speaker: Marcus
segments.text: Cyclists complained that the low lights produced a repeated flicker as they passed, which pedestrians had barely noticed. Our first adjustment reduced the effect but directed light into bedroom windows. The final shields took three attempts. That experience reminded us that a solution can transfer discomfort from one group to another unless different users test it under real conditions.

segments.speaker: Host
segments.text: The council eventually made the scheme permanent, but it did not use residents' feelings as the only measure.

segments.speaker: Marcus
segments.text: Perceived safety improved markedly, yet we also counted evening walking trips and reviewed reports of near collisions. Walking increased without a rise in incidents. We cannot claim the lamps alone caused every change, because a late bus service began during the same period. Still, the combination of observations, behaviour and safety records gave a more credible picture than a satisfaction survey on its own.

segments.speaker: Host
segments.text: For Marcus, the project offers a lesson beyond lighting.

segments.speaker: Marcus
segments.text: Public requests often describe a proposed solution—more lamps—rather than the experience underneath it—the inability to see what lies ahead. Designers should investigate that experience before committing to equipment. Consultation is most useful when it changes the question, not when it merely asks people to approve a finished answer.

items.question: What did the initial investigation show?

options.text: Residents preferred complete darkness to strong lighting
Poor visibility transitions mattered more than brightness alone
Vegetation had little effect on people's sense of safety
The station route was objectively more dangerous than reported

items.explanationZh: 居民不是一律害怕暗處，而是怕明暗落差、遮蔽物造成看不清前方；問題比單純亮度更複雜。

distractorRationales.A: 沒有偏好全暗。
distractorRationales.C: 過度生長的植物是重要因素。
distractorRationales.D: 研究談感受與視覺條件，沒有證明客觀危險較高。

items.evidence: sudden contrasts prevented them from seeing who was ahead

items.question: Why was one nearby street left unchanged?

options.text: The council had not received permission to work there
It provided a comparison for interpreting the trial
Residents there objected to temporary equipment
Its existing lights had recently been replaced

items.explanationZh: 未改造街道作為比較條件，協助區分設計效果與季節、通勤時間等其他變化。

distractorRationales.A: 沒有權限問題。
distractorRationales.C: 不是因居民反對。

items.evidence: Comparing the two routes helped us separate the effect of the design

items.question: What problem emerged during the trial?

options.text: A change that helped pedestrians caused difficulties for other users
Temporary equipment was repeatedly damaged by cyclists
Residents disliked the removal of plants from the route
Lower lamps made collisions more frequent

items.explanationZh: 行人幾乎沒注意的低燈閃爍讓騎士不適，後續調整又影響住戶，顯示不同使用者需求可能衝突。

distractorRationales.B: 沒有設備遭破壞。
distractorRationales.C: 沒有反對修剪植物。

items.evidence: Cyclists complained that the low lights produced a repeated flicker

items.question: Why is Marcus cautious about attributing changes to the lighting?

options.text: The project collected too few resident comments
No safety information was available before the trial
Another transport change occurred at the same time
The comparison street received different vegetation work

items.explanationZh: 同期新增晚班公車，可能也增加夜間步行，因此不能把所有變化都歸因於照明。

distractorRationales.A: 居民意見不少。
distractorRationales.B: 有檢視安全與事故資料。
distractorRationales.D: 沒有提比較街道的植被改造。

items.evidence: a late bus service began during the same period

items.question: What general principle does Marcus emphasise?

options.text: Public projects should follow the most popular proposed solution
Designers should uncover the need behind a requested intervention
Consultation is most reliable after equipment has been installed
Technical measurements should replace descriptions of experience

items.explanationZh: 民眾常用「多裝燈」描述解法，設計者應先釐清背後的體驗與需求，再選擇介入方式。

distractorRationales.A: 他反對直接照做提案。
distractorRationales.C: 諮詢應在定案前影響問題。
distractorRationales.D: 他主張結合體驗與量測，不是取代。

items.evidence: investigate that experience before committing to equipment

sets.title: Weather records from city balconies
sets.directions: Listen to the extended recording and answer the five questions. The information follows the question order.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.voiceCue: Neutral British woman; clear exam pace
segments.text: You hear an interviewer speaking to a scientist who runs a citizen weather project.

segments.speaker: Interviewer
segments.text: Dr Ahmed, why collect weather information from residents when the city already has an official station?

segments.speaker: Dr Ahmed
segments.voiceCue: British Pakistani woman, 40s; precise but approachable
segments.text: The official station is extremely accurate, but it sits in an open park. Most residents experience heat between buildings, above paved courtyards or on shaded streets. Temperatures can differ considerably across a few kilometres. Our volunteers do not replace the official station; their measurements reveal local patterns that a single reference point cannot show.

segments.speaker: Interviewer
segments.text: You began by lending inexpensive sensors to anyone who applied. What went wrong?

segments.speaker: Dr Ahmed
segments.text: Many people placed them where installation was convenient—on a sunny windowsill or beside an air-conditioning outlet. Those readings reflected the building more than the neighbourhood. We considered rejecting imperfect locations, but that would have excluded many flats. Instead, volunteers now photograph the site and record when it receives direct sun. We use that context to interpret the data and identify readings that require caution.

segments.speaker: Interviewer
segments.text: How do you keep volunteers interested after the novelty disappears?

segments.speaker: Dr Ahmed
segments.text: At first we sent monthly graphs covering the whole city. People liked them but could not see why their own contribution mattered. We redesigned the report so each volunteer sees their street alongside two contrasting locations. A short note explains which observation helped confirm an unusual pattern. Retention improved once contributors could recognise a connection between their small action and the larger result.

segments.speaker: Interviewer
segments.text: Did the project reveal anything the team did not expect?

segments.speaker: Dr Ahmed
segments.text: We expected the hottest places to be the densest commercial streets. Some were, but several housing estates remained warmer throughout the night. Daytime shade had hidden how much heat their concrete surfaces stored. That matters because health warnings often focus on afternoon temperatures, while people in those homes may recover poorly overnight.

segments.speaker: Interviewer
segments.text: How is the information being used now?

segments.speaker: Dr Ahmed
segments.text: The public-health team is testing whether evening outreach should target the persistent hot spots, and planners are comparing tree-planting proposals with our maps. We are careful not to promise that a few trees will solve every location. The project is most valuable as a way to decide where detailed professional surveys and community conversations should happen next.

items.question: What is the main value of the volunteers' measurements?

options.text: They provide legally recognised replacements for official records
They show variation within environments where people actually live
They are more precise than instruments in open spaces
They allow the city to stop maintaining its main station

items.explanationZh: 官方站精準但位置單一；居民感受到的是建築、鋪面與陰影造成的局部差異，志工資料補足空間分布。

distractorRationales.A: 錄音明說不取代官方站。
distractorRationales.C: 沒有宣稱較精準。

items.evidence: reveal local patterns that a single reference point cannot show

items.question: How did the team respond to unsuitable sensor locations?

options.text: They limited participation to houses with gardens
They moved every sensor to a public building
They recorded site conditions to qualify the readings
They adjusted all warm readings by the same amount

items.explanationZh: 團隊沒有排除公寓住戶，而是記錄安裝環境與日照，讓資料能被有條件地解讀。

distractorRationales.A: 此作法正是為避免排除公寓。
distractorRationales.B: 感測器仍在志工住處。

items.evidence: photograph the site and record when it receives direct sun

items.question: What increased volunteers' continued participation?

options.text: Receiving payment for each unusual reading
Seeing how their own data contributed to a comparison
Competing to record the city's highest temperature
Getting technical training in equipment repair

items.explanationZh: 把個別街道放入對照並說明其貢獻後，志工看見自己資料的意義，因此較願意持續。

distractorRationales.A: 沒有報酬制度。
distractorRationales.C: 不是競賽。

items.evidence: recognise a connection between their small action and the larger result

items.question: What finding surprised the researchers?

options.text: Commercial districts cooled faster than all residential areas
Some residential areas retained heat after daytime conditions improved
Official warnings consistently exaggerated afternoon temperatures
Concrete surfaces had little relationship with night-time heat

items.explanationZh: 部分住宅區白天看似有遮蔭，混凝土卻在夜間持續放熱，造成居民無法降溫恢復。

distractorRationales.A: 不是所有商業區都較快降溫。
distractorRationales.C: 沒有說警報誇大。

items.evidence: housing estates remained warmer throughout the night

items.question: How does Dr Ahmed view the project's role in planning?

options.text: It identifies where more detailed investigation should be focused
It proves that tree planting is the best solution everywhere
It provides enough evidence to redesign neighbourhoods immediately
It should remain separate from public-health decisions

items.explanationZh: 這些地圖主要用來決定後續專業調查與社區討論的優先地點，而非直接證明單一解法。

sets.title: Designing a quieter museum visit
sets.directions: Listen to the extended recording and answer the five questions. The information follows the question order.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.voiceCue: Neutral British woman; clear exam pace
segments.text: You hear a museum podcast featuring an access-programme manager.

segments.speaker: Host
segments.text: Samira, the museum's quiet mornings are often described as sessions for people who are sensitive to noise. Was noise the original reason for introducing them?

segments.speaker: Samira
segments.text: Noise was part of it, but families told us that unpredictability was more difficult. A school group might suddenly enter, a demonstration could begin without warning, or a gallery might close just as a visitor had prepared to enter it. The first goal was therefore to make the environment easier to anticipate, not to promise complete silence.

segments.speaker: Host
segments.text: What changes did that involve?

segments.speaker: Samira
segments.text: We publish a visual route showing which galleries will be open, where lighting changes and where visitors can take a break. During the session we pause public announcements and avoid moving large equipment. Yet we keep ordinary background sounds in the online preview. Removing them from the recording would create a false expectation and could make the real visit more stressful.

segments.speaker: Host
segments.text: The programme originally used a separate entrance. Why did you stop?

segments.speaker: Samira
segments.text: We thought a side entrance would reduce crowds. It did, but several visitors said it made the event feel hidden and required a longer route from accessible parking. We now open the main entrance fifteen minutes early for quiet-morning visitors. Staff form a clear queue before general admission begins, so the arrival is calmer without implying that the group should be kept out of sight.

segments.speaker: Host
segments.text: How do staff support people inside the galleries?

segments.speaker: Samira
segments.text: Our first training focused on recognising visible signs of distress. That was too narrow. Some visitors speak less when overwhelmed; others ask many detailed questions or move continuously. Staff now offer concrete choices—such as a quieter route or a place to sit—without demanding an explanation. The visitor decides whether an option is helpful.

segments.speaker: Host
segments.text: What are you evaluating next?

segments.speaker: Samira
segments.text: Attendance is rising, but numbers do not tell us whether visitors can engage with the collection in the way they hoped. Our new feedback asks people to choose a personal aim before the visit, perhaps spending time with one painting or remaining for forty minutes. Afterwards they can say whether the conditions supported that aim. This avoids judging success against a single idea of what a proper museum visit looks like.

items.question: What need most influenced the original design of quiet mornings?

options.text: Providing an entirely silent building
Making the visit more predictable
Preventing children from entering galleries
Keeping every exhibition open for longer

items.explanationZh: 家庭反映最困難的是突發團體、示範與臨時閉館等不可預期性，因此首要目標是可預測。

distractorRationales.C: 不是禁止兒童。
distractorRationales.D: 沒有延長所有展覽開放。

items.question: Why are ordinary background sounds included in the online preview?

To train staff to notice equipment noise

items.explanationZh: 保留一般環境聲，是避免把線上預覽做得過度安靜，讓訪客對現場有真實預期。

sets.title: How residents redesigned a common room
sets.directions: Listen to the extended recording and answer the five questions. The information follows the question order.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.voiceCue: Neutral British woman; clear exam pace
segments.text: You hear a presenter interviewing a resident of a cooperative housing project.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: Nora, your building was designed with a large common room. How did residents expect to use it?

segments.speaker: Nora
segments.text: The architects imagined shared dinners and large meetings, so the room had one enormous table and very little else. Residents liked the idea in principle, but booking the whole room felt excessive for two people having coffee. Because the furniture could not be moved easily, smaller groups often stayed in their flats. The impressive room was empty most evenings.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: What prompted a redesign?

segments.speaker: Nora
segments.text: A temporary heating failure was unexpectedly useful. We brought in portable lamps and borrowed small tables so people could work in the warmer common room. Different activities happened at once without conflict. That made us realise the failure was not a lack of community spirit; the layout offered only one scale of gathering.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: How did you decide what permanent changes to make?

segments.speaker: Nora
segments.text: Rather than vote on a catalogue, we observed the temporary arrangement for six weeks. Residents placed a card on the table describing what they were doing and whether they wanted others to join. We discovered that people valued a mix: one open table for sociable activities, two quieter corners and storage that allowed chairs to be rearranged quickly. The cards also showed that some apparently private activities became social when joining was clearly invited.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: Were there concerns about fairness?

segments.speaker: Nora
segments.text: Yes. Frequent users initially argued that they should control the schedule because they understood the room best. Less visible residents replied that fixed evening bookings excluded shift workers. We now protect several unbooked periods and publish usage by time rather than by name. That lets us notice neglected hours without making individuals feel monitored.

segments.speaker: Presenter
segments.text: What lesson would you offer other housing projects?

segments.speaker: Nora
segments.text: Do not measure success by how often a room is occupied. Constant use can mean a small group has taken possession. We ask whether different residents can shape the space, whether someone can join without advance planning and whether quiet use is respected alongside lively events. Shared space works when it supports several forms of belonging, not when it forces everyone to socialise in the same way.

items.question: Why was the common room initially underused?

options.text: Residents objected to sharing meals with neighbours
Its design suited only relatively large activities
The building charged residents to reserve it
Its location was inconvenient for most flats

items.explanationZh: 巨大固定桌使空間只適合大型聚會，小團體覺得訂整間太誇張，因此很少使用。

distractorRationales.C: 沒有收費。
distractorRationales.D: 問題在家具與規模，不在位置。

items.evidence: smaller groups often stayed in their flats

items.question: What did the heating failure reveal?

options.text: Residents preferred working alone in warmer flats
Temporary flexible furniture supported simultaneous uses
Portable lighting was the building's most urgent need
Large meetings created fewer conflicts than small gatherings

items.explanationZh: 供暖故障迫使大家搬入小桌與可移動設備，意外證明彈性配置能讓不同活動並存。

distractorRationales.A: 人們反而在公共空間一起工作。
distractorRationales.C: 燈具只是臨時設備，不是主要發現。
distractorRationales.D: 發現的是多種小活動可並存。

items.evidence: Different activities happened at once without conflict

items.question: Why did residents use activity cards during the trial?

options.text: To collect evidence about actual patterns of use
To charge different rates for different activities

To identify who had moved furniture without permission

items.explanationZh: 卡片記錄活動與是否歡迎加入，讓設計決策建立在六週真實使用模式，而非只看目錄投票。

distractorRationales.B: 沒有費率。
distractorRationales.C: 卡片也可明確邀請加入，不是全面阻止。

items.evidence: describing what they were doing and whether they wanted others to join

items.question: How did the project respond to concerns about access?

options.text: It gave frequent users permanent booking priority
It stopped accepting reservations in the evening
It kept some time available without prior booking

distractorRationales.B: 不是全面禁止晚間預約。

items.evidence: protect several unbooked periods

items.question: What does Nora consider a better sign of success than constant occupancy?

options.text: Residents using the room for the same purpose each week
A wide range of people being able to influence how it works
Every activity attracting as many participants as possible
Social events gradually replacing quiet individual use

items.explanationZh: 她重視不同居民是否能塑造空間、臨時加入，以及安靜與熱鬧用途並存，而非單純高使用率。

distractorRationales.C: 不是所有活動都要多人參加。
distractorRationales.D: 安靜使用同樣應被尊重。

sets.title: Five people change how they travel
sets.directions: Listen to five speakers. Match each speaker with the factor that helped the new travel habit continue.

segments.speaker: Narrator
segments.voiceCue: Neutral British woman; clear exam pace
segments.text: Five people describe a change in the way they travel around their city.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: I had tried cycling to work before, but I spent the whole day worrying about leaving an expensive bicycle outside the office. The journey itself was pleasant and the traffic was manageable. What changed things was our building converting an unused storeroom into a locked cycle area. Once I knew the bicycle and wet clothing had somewhere safe to stay, cycling became my normal choice.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: The bus route was always there, yet I avoided it because the printed timetable did not reflect congestion. I hated standing at the stop without knowing whether a bus was two minutes or twenty minutes away. The live map now shows its actual position. The service is not faster, but the uncertainty has gone, so I can plan when to leave home.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Walking to the market seemed sensible, but it was easy to postpone on cold mornings. Then a neighbour suggested that we go together every Saturday. Neither of us wants to disappoint the other, and the conversation makes the forty-minute journey feel shorter. I still walk alone during the week sometimes, but the regular shared trip is what established the habit.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: I liked the idea of giving up short car journeys, but ordinary bicycles could not carry the weekly food shop. A community project lent me a cargo bicycle with a large front box. Being able to transport heavy bags meant the change worked for real errands, not just leisure rides. I eventually bought a second-hand model from another member.

segments.speaker: Speaker 5
segments.text: An electric bicycle sounded suitable for the hills near my flat, although I was reluctant to spend so much on something I might dislike. The local shop offered a week-long loan and adjusted the bicycle to my route. That trial showed me which battery size I actually needed and removed the risk of making an expensive mistake.

A regular commitment to another person
An opportunity to test equipment before purchase

sets.title: Meeting-free mornings
sets.directions: Read the article and answer the five questions.

stimulus.text:
Case study: testing an assumption

A software team reserved two mornings a week for uninterrupted work. Managers expected employees to resist losing flexible meeting times. Yet the first review produced an awkward finding. Calendar data showed that fragmented attention, not total meeting hours, caused most delays.

The group did not move directly from concern to permanent policy. The team tested fixed collaboration periods in the afternoons. The choice had a practical basis: people still had daily opportunities to discuss urgent work. During the trial, some clients continued requesting morning calls. That complication was logged rather than treated as a reason to abandon the work.

The closing review found that project tasks were completed earlier without reducing client contact. The organisers compared this outcome with their original expectation and with comments from the people affected. Their final lesson was that protected time works only when an alternative contact window is clear. They recommended another evidence check before the approach was transferred elsewhere.

The meeting-free mornings review concerned work patterns, but the team deliberately kept its claim narrow. In this work patterns case, records were dated, comments were checked against observations, and disagreements were retained so that the final account would not describe only the most favourable experience.

options.text: to explain how evidence changed the approach to meeting-free mornings
to advertise meeting-free mornings as a solution for every organisation
to argue that collecting evidence delays useful action

distractorRationales.B: 「to advertise meeting-free mornings as a solution for every organisation」與原文線索「Calendar data showed that fragmented attention, not total meeting hours, caused most delays. The team tested fixed collaboration periods in the afternoons.」不一致。
distractorRationales.C: 「to argue that collecting evidence delays useful action」與原文線索「Calendar data showed that fragmented attention, not total meeting hours, caused most delays. The team tested fixed collaboration periods in the afternoons.」不一致。

items.evidence: Calendar data showed that fragmented attention, not total meeting hours, caused most delays. The team tested fixed collaboration periods in the afternoons.

options.text: It rejects the measured result in favour of the original assumption.
It turns a local finding into cautious guidance without claiming universal proof.
It focuses on a difficulty that the trial did not actually encounter.

distractorRationales.C: 「It focuses on a difficulty that the trial did not actually encounter.」與原文線索「protected time works only when an alternative contact window is clear」不一致。

stimulus.text:
Internal evaluation memo

Issue under review
A customer team piloted one senior role shared by two experienced employees.

Initial position
Leaders feared customers would receive inconsistent decisions.

Evidence received
Early monitoring showed handover quality depended on shared records, not one named contact. This evidence mattered because it described what was actually happening, not what the team expected to happen.

Response and constraints
The partners used a common decision log and a fifteen-minute overlap each day. It was selected because both employees could see the reasoning behind previous actions Implementation was not completely smooth: urgent cases sometimes arrived outside the overlap period

Decision note
Response consistency improved and neither employee accumulated excessive overtime. The review therefore records one main conclusion: shared responsibility succeeds when decision history is visible The result supports a next step, but it is not presented as proof that every department or community would obtain the same outcome.

For job-sharing pilot, the organisers agreed in advance what would count as a useful result. The job-sharing pilot record also includes unexpected effects, since a change can solve one problem while creating another that is less visible in an overall average.

sets.directions: Read the article and answer the five questions.

stimulus.text:
Interview with the project lead

Q: What prompted the review?
A: A service company discovered that its satisfaction survey produced little useful guidance. Managers thought adding more questions would provide richer data.

Q: When did that view begin to change?
A: Customers often abandoned the long form and remaining answers came from extreme opinions.

Q: What did you do next?
A: Researchers reduced it to six questions and invited a rotating sample. We chose that route because a shorter representative survey was more useful than a large biased one.

Q: Was the change easy to introduce?
A: No. teams disagreed about which historical questions to remove

Q: And what did the final evidence show?
A: completion increased and moderate opinions became more visible

Q: What should another team take from this?
A: Our strongest conclusion is that measurement quality depends on who responds as well as what is asked. But another setting should still test its own assumptions instead of copying our decision automatically.

Because the case involved research, several groups were affected in different ways. The a better customer survey report therefore distinguishes direct measurements from personal preferences and explains which conclusions depend on the particular setting in which the trial took place.

sets.title: Cafeteria price display
sets.directions: Read the article and answer the five questions.

stimulus.text:
A small change with measurable consequences

A workplace cafeteria changed how meal prices were displayed. The operator assumed customers mainly wanted lower prices. The data, however, pointed in a different direction. Feedback showed people were frustrated by discovering optional charges at the till.

Rather than debate the issue indefinitely, menus began showing one complete price and clearly marked paid extras. The experiment was designed this way because price certainty could improve trust without reducing food quality. One weakness soon became visible—the till system needed several weeks of reprogramming—so the team documented when and where that problem occurred.

By the end, complaints fell even though average prices changed very little. That did not settle every question, but it gave the discussion firmer ground. The people running the project now argue that clarity can matter as much as the absolute price. Their report distinguishes between the measured result and benefits that supporters merely hoped the change would produce.

The account of cafeteria price display draws on a limited review period. Its cafeteria price display timeline includes the original plan, observations made during delivery and a later comparison, allowing readers to see where interpretation begins rather than treating every comment as equivalent evidence.

stimulus.text:
Project diary

Week 1 — The question
A technical apprenticeship added short rotations through three departments. Supervisors feared brief placements would produce only superficial learning.

Week 2 — A surprise
Apprentices could explain systems better after seeing how departments depended on one another. We realised that our explanation rested more on habit than on recent information.

Weeks 3–6 — The trial
Each rotation used one practical question linking work to the next team. The reasoning was that a focused question gave short placements a clear purpose A difficulty appeared almost immediately: departments initially selected tasks requiring too much prior knowledge We kept the trial running but noted the limitation.

Final week — What changed
final project proposals became more realistic and collaborative Looking back, the most useful lesson was that breadth becomes useful when learners connect experiences explicitly The diary will be reviewed again after a longer period to see whether the improvement lasts.

The apprenticeships project was not evaluated only by the people who designed it. Participants in apprentice rotation were invited to identify disadvantages, and the final record preserves points on which the group did not reach agreement.

stimulus.text:
Briefing for decision-makers

Purpose: to decide whether an established approach still matched current needs. A company redesigned the first week for new office employees.

Managers assumed newcomers needed every policy explained before doing real work. That position became difficult to maintain once the review found that feedback showed that long presentations were forgotten before the information became relevant.

The recommended test was specific: the company replaced several lectures with guided tasks and short reference cards. It offered a reasonable way forward because employees could learn a rule when they first needed to apply it. The risk log also records that trainers had to prepare realistic examples without exposing confidential data.

The trial produced a useful but limited result: new staff completed routine work sooner and asked more focused questions. On that basis, the briefing recommends treating the following as the guiding principle—orientation is more memorable when information is connected to immediate action—while continuing to collect evidence before a wider rollout.

Before the a shorter first week decision was confirmed, the team checked whether the apparent improvement could have another explanation. That a shorter first week check did not remove every uncertainty, but it made the recommendation more precise and easier to test later.

stimulus.text:
Independent observer's note

I joined the project after its members had already agreed on the likely cause of the problem. A consultancy changed how it reviewed major client proposals. Partners assumed senior approval near the deadline provided adequate quality control. Soon afterwards, though, post-project reviews found that weak assumptions had rarely been questioned early enough.

The group responded by taking a reversible step. A small challenge panel now reviews evidence before the final document is written. Their explanation for the choice was that early criticism is cheaper to address than late rewriting. From an observer's perspective, the main operational weakness was clear: proposal teams sometimes treated questions as opposition rather than support.

When the figures were reviewed, fewer claims required correction and final reviews became faster. My reading of the evidence is close to the team's own conclusion: constructive challenge works best before a team becomes attached to its solution. What deserves praise is not simply the outcome, but the willingness to revise an attractive explanation when the facts did not support it.

In this proposal review case, success was defined before the trial began. The a challenge panel for proposals organisers compared the final evidence with that definition instead of selecting whichever result made the change appear most successful.

sets.title: A clearer shift handover
sets.directions: Read the article and answer the five questions.

stimulus.text:
Retrospective: from certainty to evidence

A laboratory reviewed errors that occurred between evening and morning shifts. Team leaders assumed adding more detail to the handover document would solve the problem. That confidence faded when staff found that long notes hid the few decisions requiring immediate attention.

The team then asked what it could test without committing to a permanent redesign. Its answer was to proceed as follows: the new format separates urgent actions, unresolved questions and background information. The idea was defensible because readers could identify priorities before reviewing supporting detail. Even so, workers needed practice deciding which category an issue belonged in.

At the retrospective meeting, the most important result was that missed follow-ups decreased and handovers took less time. Participants disagreed about some secondary benefits, so those claims were left out of the final recommendation. What remained was a more cautious lesson: effective records make priority visible instead of simply adding information.

The evidence in the shift work review comes from one local context. For a clearer shift handover, its value lies in showing why a decision was made and what happened next, not in promising that another group will obtain an identical result.

sets.directions: Read the article and answer the five questions.

stimulus.text:
Research digest

Question: A construction firm investigated repeated disputes about supplier payment dates.

Working hypothesis: Accounts staff believed the contract wording already explained the process sufficiently.

Contrary observation: Suppliers could not see when a disputed invoice had moved to another reviewer.

Method: A status page now shows the responsible team and the next required action. This method was selected because visibility helps suppliers respond before a minor issue becomes a long delay

Limitation: internal teams first used inconsistent labels for the same approval stage

What we changed—and why

The problem
Residents opened a shared fridge for surplus food.

What we used to believe

Donations arrived quickly, but unclear labels caused safe food to be discarded.

Retrospective: from certainty to evidence

Students mapped local places that repair everyday objects. They assumed a simple list of addresses would be enough. That confidence faded when users wanted to know which materials, brands and ages each shop accepted.

Research digest

Question: A museum invited visitors to comment on object labels.

Working hypothesis: Curators assumed unfamiliar technical terms caused most confusion.

Contrary observation: Visitors understood individual words but often missed why an object mattered.

Limitation: some important objects had very limited historical records

In rewriting museum labels, this helps decision-makers judge whether an improvement is large enough to justify the practical cost of introducing the change. Further evidence about rewriting museum labels will be collected so that the museums conclusion can be checked over a longer period.

Residents discussed adding lights to a path through a local park. Supporters assumed brighter lighting would make everyone feel safer. Yet the first review produced an awkward finding. Evening walks showed glare created dark areas beyond each lamp and disturbed wildlife.

stimulus.text:
Project diary

Week 1 — The question
A library wanted its reading group to include adults rebuilding reading confidence. Existing members assumed everyone should finish the entire book before meeting.

Week 2 — A surprise
New participants contributed more when short selected sections were discussed first. We realised that our explanation rested more on habit than on recent information.

Weeks 3–6 — The trial
Meetings now begin with a shared extract before opening wider conversation. The reasoning was that a common manageable starting point reduces fear of being unprepared A difficulty appeared almost immediately: regular members worried that discussion would become less challenging We kept the trial running but noted the limitation.

Final week — What changed
attendance widened while optional full-book conversations continued Looking back, the most useful lesson was that inclusive participation can be created without limiting deeper engagement The diary will be reviewed again after a longer period to see whether the improvement lasts.

The reading groups project was not evaluated only by the people who designed it. Participants in a welcoming reading group were invited to identify disadvantages, and the final record preserves points on which the group did not reach agreement.

stimulus.text:
Briefing for decision-makers

Purpose: to decide whether an established approach still matched current needs. Researchers examined how street trees affected temperatures across a city.

They expected neighbourhoods with the most trees to be consistently coolest. That position became difficult to maintain once the review found that measurements showed shade location and paved surface area changed the effect throughout the day.

The recommended test was specific: the study compared repeated route temperatures with detailed maps of surrounding surfaces. It offered a reasonable way forward because local arrangement could explain variation hidden by total tree counts. The risk log also records that portable sensors were influenced briefly by traffic and building exhaust.

The trial produced a useful but limited result: the team identified locations where additional shade would have the greatest benefit. On that basis, the briefing recommends treating the following as the guiding principle—environmental planning needs spatial evidence rather than one city-wide average—while continuing to collect evidence before a wider rollout.

Before the where street trees cool most decision was confirmed, the team checked whether the apparent improvement could have another explanation. That where street trees cool most check did not remove every uncertainty, but it made the recommendation more precise and easier to test later.

stimulus.text:
Independent observer's note

I joined the project after its members had already agreed on the likely cause of the problem. Travellers created an online map of public drinking-water points. Contributors assumed adding as many locations as possible would make the map useful. Soon afterwards, though, users arrived at fountains that were seasonal, inaccessible or temporarily broken.

The group responded by taking a reversible step. Each entry gained an access description and a date when someone last confirmed it. Their explanation for the choice was that current practical details were more valuable than an impressive total. From an observer's perspective, the main operational weakness was clear: popular locations needed checking more often than remote ones.

When the figures were reviewed, failed journeys decreased and volunteers focused updates where demand was highest. My reading of the evidence is close to the team's own conclusion: crowdsourced information needs visible freshness and verification. What deserves praise is not simply the outcome, but the willingness to revise an attractive explanation when the facts did not support it.

In this public information case, success was defined before the trial began. The a reliable water-refill map organisers compared the final evidence with that definition instead of selecting whichever result made the change appear most successful.

items.question: Which interpretation of the result in “A reliable water-refill map” is best supported?

options.text: The result guarantees that the same method will succeed elsewhere.
The trial produced useful local evidence, although some questions remain open.
The outcome was based entirely on participants' predictions.

items.explanationZh: 關鍵線索是「failed journeys decreased and volunteers focused updates where demand was highest」，因此應選「The trial produced useful local evidence, although some questions remain open.」。
